cues.say: A rate limit is a cap on how often one person or machine can call you, say ten requests a second. Anything over the cap gets an instant error that says: slow down.
That error is HTTP status four twenty-nine: too many requests. You rarely build the first layer yourself. Your CDN or firewall offers it as a setting.
Why do you need it? An electronics sale opens. A reseller's script hits checkout three hundred times a second, from one IP address.
It floods your servers, and buys the TVs before real customers can click.
And it's not always on purpose. A buggy app that retries in a tight loop can turn one small hiccup into an outage.
The usual way to enforce a limit is a token bucket. Each IP address gets a bucket of ten tokens, refilled at ten a second. Every request spends one.
A normal customer spends a few, and the bucket refills. They never notice.
The script empties its bucket in a blink. Every request after that, with no token left, gets a four twenty-nine, without ever reaching your servers.
A well-behaved client reads that error, waits, and tries again later.
So it protects you from bots, and from retry storms: the buggy loop gets errors, not your database.
It also keeps you under other people's limits. Stripe allows about a hundred requests a second, so you cap your own calls.
Back to the sale. With an edge cap of ten a second per IP, two hundred and ninety of the script's three hundred requests are rejected before your servers.
But the script can switch IP addresses. So the API also caps orders per customer: two per phone number, whatever the IP.
Here's where it sits. The per IP cap runs at the edge, in the CDN and its web application firewall, or WAF.
The business cap lives in the API, where it knows who the customer is.
Two things to know. An office or a mobile carrier can put many real people behind one IP, so leave room in the cap.
And per IP alone is easy to dodge, because scripts rotate addresses. The per-customer cap catches that.
In the interview, say: per IP at the edge, and two orders per phone in the API.
